summary: Summarizes current practices, problems, and solutions for multipath routing, where a router has several next hops for a destination and must pick one for each packet.

eli5.summary: When a router has several equally good roads, it must choose one. This discusses the ways to choose and their problems.

questions: why is round robin bad for multipath routing
what is highest random weight hashing
hash threshold vs modulo n next hop
subtitle: Why a router with several equally good routes should not just pick a next hop at random, and which selection methods work better.

tldr.problem: When a router has several equal-cost next hops for a destination, naive choices like round-robin or random split one flow across paths, which breaks path MTU discovery, reorders packets, hurts TCP and confuses debugging tools.
tldr.mechanism: Keep every packet of a flow on the same path by hashing the flow's header fields. The memo compares modulo-N hash, hash-threshold and Highest Random Weight (HRW).
tldr.outcome: It recommends HRW when the forwarder keeps per-flow state (and always for multicast) and hash-threshold when it does not. It is an Informational memo, not a standard.

facts.label: Fast-retransmit trigger
facts.value: 3 or more later packets arrive first

today: RFC 2991 is an Informational memo from November 2000, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion to RFC 2992, which analyses the hash-threshold method.

sections.title: Problems With Naive Multipath
sections.content:
Routing protocols such as OSPF and ISIS explicitly allow Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP), and some routers also use it with RIP and other protocols. A forwarder then has several next hops for a destination and needs a method to choose one for each packet. A naive approach is round-robin, where each packet takes the next next-hop in turn. It balances load, but round-robin and random choice share several problems.

  • Variable path MTU: each path may have a different MTU, so the overall path MTU can change packet by packet, which defeats path MTU discovery.
  • Variable latencies: packets can arrive out of order. TCP treats late packets as loss and enters fast-retransmit after three or more packets arrive before a late one, wasting bandwidth.
  • Debugging: tools such as ping and traceroute become less reliable and may show completely wrong results.

Multicast has a different problem. DVMRP, PIM-DM and PIM-SM build a single tree per group to avoid loops and duplicates, so a tree must use only a single next-hop towards its root.
sections.eli5: If your family's cars take different roads, they arrive in a jumbled order and the map app gets confused. It is better if every car from the same trip uses the same road.

sections.title: What a Good Method Needs
sections.content:
The memo uses flow to mean the granularity at which the router keeps state, if at all. A flow might be just a destination address, or a (source address, destination address, protocol id) triplet. It is not necessarily the same as a microflow in RFC 2474, which also includes port numbers. Including transport-layer information can be problematic: fragmented packets may not carry it, and it can undo the benefit of caching MTU information between the same endpoints.

The natural solution is to make sure that packets of the same flow always use the same path. Two further features are desirable:

  • Minimal disruption: adding or removing a next hop should affect as few active flows as possible, because route flaps matter more when many routes carry traffic.
  • Fast implementation: the extra work per packet should be small, like incrementing an index modulo the number of next hops.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: keep each trip on one road. When a road opens or closes, as few trips as possible should have to change, and picking a road should be quick.

sections.title: Three Ways to Pick a Next Hop
sections.content:
The RFC describes three methods that keep a flow on one path.

Modulo-N hash: hash the flow's header fields and take the result modulo N, the number of next hops. It is fast, but (N-1)/N of all flows change path whenever a next hop is added or removed.

Hash-threshold: hash the flow fields to get a key. Each of the N next hops owns a region of the hash output space, and the region containing the key picks the next hop. For ECMP the lookup is a simple division (hash_value / fixed_region_size). When a next hop is added or removed, between 1/4 and 1/2 of all flows change paths. The analysis is in RFC 2992.

Highest Random Weight (HRW): for each next hop, hash the flow fields together with the next hop's address and choose the next hop with the highest result. Only 1/N of flows are affected by an addition or deletion, but it costs roughly N times as much as a modulo-N hash.
sections.eli5: Modulo-N is a quick shuffle that reassigns almost everyone when a road changes. Hash-threshold gives each road a slice of a number line, so only people near the edges move. HRW lets every road bid and picks the top bidder, which moves the fewest people but takes the longest.

sections.title: Unicast, Multicast and Parallel Links
sections.content:
Which method fits depends on whether the forwarder keeps per-flow state and how precious CPU is. With per-flow state the next hop is computed once at state creation, so any method works, but hash-based ones are better because the same path is chosen again if state is deleted. For path stability the RFC recommends HRW. Without per-flow state the next hop must be computed for every packet, and when CPU matters more than path stability, hash-threshold is recommended.

For unicast, the memo recommends HRW at state creation (and next-hop deletion) time where flow state exists, and hash-threshold otherwise. Multicast forwarders always keep per-flow state, so the router should always use HRW. Routers using explicit-join protocols such as PIM-SM should use multipath information when choosing where to send a join, for example using HRW per group when there are several next hops toward the Rendezvous Point.

Hash methods only spread flows evenly when the hash is uniformly distributed, which needs a large number of inputs, so they suit routers that carry many flows better than a small business setting. Parallel links between the same two routers can be bundled into a "super"-link, which reduces multicast to one next hop. A method is still needed to pick the physical link, and round-robin can still reorder packets and hurt TCP.
sections.eli5: If the router keeps notes about each trip, it can afford the careful bidding method. If it keeps no notes and has to hurry, the number-line slices are the better choice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo does not directly affect the security of the Internet infrastructure. It does note one risk: when next-hop selection is predictable, an attacker can build traffic that all hashes the same and overload one path in a denial-of-service attack. The easiest case is when only a single next hop is ever used, so introducing multipath can make such an attack harder, and the less predictable the hash, the harder it is to attack any one link.
sections.eli5: If a bad guy knows exactly which road each trip will take, he can send a crowd all down the same road to jam it. Mixing the choices in a hard-to-guess way makes that harder.
